title.en: Hsü Wu Kuei Judges of Dogs and Horses (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 徐無鬼見魏武侯：相狗相馬（莊子）

region.en: The Wei court (Anyang region, Henan, China)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: The hermit Hsü Wu Kuei, sympathising with the prince rather than being pitied himself, cheers the melancholy ruler by telling how he judges dogs — the highest class as though they had parted with their own individuality — and horses: the horses of the State run to line and arc, but the horses of the Empire move as though they had lost the way, and outstrip all competitors over the unstirred dust, out of sight.
summary.zh: 徐無鬼見魏武侯，相狗相馬之術——直者中繩，曲者中鉤，此國家之馬也；若此者，絕塵弭轍，若喪其一，此天下之馬也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); tagged oracle-divination for the judge-of-horses topos (interpretive). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "It is I who should sympathise with your Highness, not your Highness with me," answered Hsü Wu Kuei. "If your Highness gives free play to passion and yields to loves and hates, then the natural conditions of your existence will suffer. ... The Prince was too astonished to reply; and after a while Hsü Wu Kuei continued, "I will try to explain to your Highness how I judge of dogs. The lowest in the scale will eat their fill and then stop, like a cat. Those of the middle class are as though staring at the sun. The highest class are as though they had parted with their own individuality.

"But I do not judge of dogs as well as I judge of horses. I judge of horses as follows. Their straightness must be that of a line. Their curve must be that of an arc. Their squareness, that of the square. Their roundness, that of the compasses. These are the horses of the State. They are not equal to the horses of the Empire. The horses of the Empire are splendid. They move as though anxious to get along, as though they had lost the way, as though they had parted with their own individuality. Thus, they outstrip all competitors, over the unstirred dust, out of sight!"

The Prince was greatly pleased and smiled. ... "Have you not heard," said Hsü Wu Kuei, "of the outlaw of Yüeh? After several days' absence from his State, he was glad to meet any one he had known there. After a month, he was glad to meet any one he had even seen there. And after a year, he was glad to meet any one who was in any way like to his fellow-countrymen. ... Long it is, I ween, since his Highness has heard the voice of a pure man at his side!"

title.en: The Divine Teacher Boy Who Governed the Empire as He Kept His Horses (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 黃帝襄城之野遇牧馬小童（莊子）

region.en: The wilds of Hsiang-ch'êng, beyond the known world (symbolic pin: Xiangcheng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 襄城之野（象徵定位：河南襄城）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: The Yellow Emperor rides to seek the Tao upon the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain with six sage companions, and all seven lose their way in the wilds of Hsiang-ch'êng. A boy grazing horses tells them where the mountain is and where the TAO abides — and how to govern the empire: just the same as I look after my horses. See that no harm comes to the horses, that is all! The Emperor prostrates himself before the boy, addressing him as Divine Teacher.
summary.zh: 黃帝將見大隗乎具茨之山——七聖皆迷，無所問塗；適遇牧馬童子。小童曰：夫為天下者，亦奚以異乎牧馬者哉？亦去其害馬者而已矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the seven-sages-lose-the-way myth and the Divine-Teacher boy. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When the Yellow Emperor went to see TAO upon the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain, Fang Ming was his charioteer, Ch'ang Yü sat on his right, Chang Jo and Hsi P'êng were his outriders, and K'un Hun and Hua Chi brought up the rear. On reaching the wilds of Hsiang-ch'êng, these seven Sages lost their way and there was no one of whom to ask the road. By and by, they fell in with a boy who was grazing horses, and asked him, saying, "Do you know the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain?" "I do," replied the boy. "And can you tell us," continued the Sages, "where TAO abides?" "I can," replied the boy.

"This is a strange lad," cried the Yellow Emperor. "Not only does he know where the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain is, but also where TAO abides! Come tell me, pray, how would you govern the empire?" "I should govern the empire," said the boy, "just the same as I look after my horses. What else should I do? "When I was a little boy and used to live within the points of the compass, my eyes got dim of sight. An old man advised me to mount the chariot of the sun and visit the wilds of Hsiang-ch'êng. My sight is now much better, and I continue to dwell without the points of the compass. I should govern the empire in just the same way. What else should I do?"

The boy declined to answer, but on being again urged, cried out, "What difference is there between governing the empire and looking after horses? See that no harm comes to the horses, that is all!" Thereupon the Emperor prostrated himself before the boy; and addressing him as Divine Teacher, took his leave.

title.en: Lu Chü's Two Lutes and the Twenty-Five Jangled Strings (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 魯遽調瑟，二十五弦皆動（莊子）

region.en: The hall and adjoining room (symbolic pin: Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 堂與室之瑟（象徵定位：山東曲阜）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: A disciple of Lu Chü boasts he can do without fire in winter and make ice in summer; Lu Chü answers by tuning two lutes, one in the hall and one in the adjoining room, so that the struck note sounds in both — then, changing one string out of the octave, he strikes it and all the twenty-five strings jangle together. There was sound as before, but the influence of the key-note was gone.
summary.zh: 魯遽曰：是直以陽召陽，以陰召陰——於是乎為之調瑟；廢一於堂，廢一於室；鼓宮宮動，鼓角角動。於是乎為之改調，一於宮宮，五音不比，二十五弦皆動。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "Thereupon he tuned two lutes, and placed one in the hall and the other in the adjoining room. And when he struck the Kung note on one, the Kung note on the other sounded; when he struck the chio note on one, the chio note on the other sounded. This because they were both tuned to the same pitch. But if he changed the interval of one string, so that it no longer kept its place in the octave, and then struck it, the result was that all the twenty-five strings jangled together. There was sound as before, but the influence of the key-note was gone. Is this your case?"

title.en: The Stone-Mason and the Scab No Thicker Than a Fly's Wing (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 匠石斲郢人之鼻堊（莊子）

region.en: Ying, capital of Ch'u (Jingzhou, Hubei, China)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: At Hui Tzŭ's grave, Chuang Tzŭ recalls the man of Ying whose nose bore a scab no thicker than a fly's wing: the stone-mason chipped it off with his adze while the patient sat unmoved, the nose uninjured. Summoned by the prince of Sung to try the same, the stone-mason answers that his material has long since perished — and I too, ever since he perished, have been without my material, having no one with whom I can speak.
summary.zh: 郢人堊漫其鼻端若蠅翼，使匠石斲之；匠石運斤成風，聽而斲之，盡堊而鼻不傷。臣嘗能之矣，雖然，臣之質死久矣！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Chuang Tzŭ was once attending a funeral, when he passed by the grave of Hui Tzŭ. Turning to his attendants, he said, "A man of Ying who had his nose covered with a hard scab, no thicker than a fly's wing, sent for a stone-mason to chip it off. The stone-mason plied his adze with great dexterity while the patient sat still and let him chip. When the scab was all off, the nose was found to be uninjured, the man of Ying never having moved a muscle.

When Yüan, prince of Sung, heard of this, he summoned the stone-mason and said, 'Try to do the same for me.' "'I used to be able to do it Sire,' replied the stone-mason, 'but my material has long since perished.' "And I too, ever since he perished, have been without my material, having no one with whom I can speak."

title.en: Kuan Chung's Deathbed Advice: It Must Be Hsi P'êng (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 管仲有病，屬國於隰朋（莊子）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: Dying Kuan Chung refuses Duke Huan's choice of Pao Yü — pure, incorruptible, he will not associate with those unlike himself — and names instead Hsi P'êng, who forgets the authority of those above him, grieves over those not the peers of himself, and hears not the things in the State he should not hear. There is no alternative; it must be Hsi P'êng.
summary.zh: 管仲有病，公曰：鮑叔牙可乎？管仲曰：不可——其為人也，潔廉善士也，其於不己若者不比之。其於國也，有不聞也；其於家也，有不見也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Kuan Chung being at the point of death, Duke Huan went to see him. "You are ill, venerable Sir," said the Duke, "really ill. You had better say to whom, in the event of your getting worse, I am to entrust the administration of the State." "Whom does your Highness wish to choose?" enquired Kuan Chung. "Will Pao Yü do?" asked the Duke. "He will not," said Kuan Chung. "He is pure, incorruptible, and good. With those who are not like himself, he will not associate. And if he has once heard of a man's wrong-doing, he never forgets it. If you employ him in the administration of the empire, he will get to loggerheads with his prince and to sixes and sevens with the people.

"There is no alternative," replied Kuan Chung; "it must be Hsi P'êng. He is a man who forgets the authority of those above him, and makes those below him forget his. Ashamed that he is not the peer of the Yellow Emperor, he grieves over those who are not the peers of himself. To share one's virtue with others is called true wisdom. To share one's wealth with others is reckoned meritorious. To exhibit superior merit is not the way to win men's hearts. To exhibit inferior merit is the way. There are things in the State he does not hear; there are things in the family he does not see. There is no alternative; it must be Hsi P'êng."

title.en: The Showing-Off Monkey of Monkey Mountain (Zhuangzi)

region.en: Monkey Mountain of Wu (symbolic pin: Zhenjiang, Jiangsu, China)
region.zh: 吳之猨山（象徵定位：江蘇鎮江）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: The monkeys of Monkey Mountain flee from the prince of Wu's shooting-party — except one which flaunts its skill and catches the flying arrow in its hand, to be killed by the guards' cloud of arrows. Beware! says the prince: do not flaunt your superiority in the faces of others. Yen Pu I goes home and studies under Tung Wu, and in three years his praise is in everybody's mouth.
summary.zh: 吳王浮於江，登乎狙之山；眾狙見之，恂然棄而逃——有一狙焉，見巧乎王；王射之，敏給搏捷矢。王命相者趨射，狙執死。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The prince of Wu took a boat and went to the Monkey Mountain, which he ascended. When the monkeys saw him, they fled in terror and hid themselves in the thicket. One of them, however, disported himself carelessly, as though showing off its skill before the prince. The prince took a shot at it; but the monkey, with great rapidity, seized the flying arrow with its hand. Then the prince bade his guards try, the result being that the monkey was killed.

Thereupon the prince turned to his friend Yen Pu I, and said, "That monkey flaunted its skill and its dexterity in my face. Therefore it has come to this pass. Beware! Do not flaunt your superiority in the faces of others." Yen Pu I went home, and put himself under the tuition of Tung Wu, with a view to get rid of such superiority. He put aside all that gave him pleasure and avoided gaining reputation. And in three years his praise was in everybody's mouth.

title.en: Chiu Fang Yin Examines the Eight Sons (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 子綦八子，九方歅相之（莊子）

region.en: The father's hall (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 父之堂（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: Tzŭ Chi summons the physiognomist Chiu Fang Yin to examine his eight sons; K'un will be the fortunate one — he will eat at the table of a prince — and the father weeps, for every uncanny effect must be preceded by some uncanny cause. Shortly afterwards K'un is captured by brigands, his feet cut off, and sold as door-keeper to Duke Chü — with meat to his dinner for the rest of his life.
summary.zh: 子綦有子八人，屬諸九方歅：楣也，必與國君同食以終其身。俄而楣到於燕，盜得之於道，刖而鬻之於齊——適為渠公之街，然食肉終身。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Tzŭ Chi had eight sons. He ranged them before him, and summoning Chiu Fang Yin, said to him, "Examine my sons physiognomically, and tell me which will be the fortunate one." "K'un," replied Chiu Fang Yin, "will be the fortunate one." "In what sense?" asked the father, beaming with delight. "K'un," said Chiu Fang Yin, "will eat at the table of a prince, and so end his days." Thereupon Tzŭ Chi burst into tears and said, "What has my son done that this should be his fate?"

"My sons and I do but roam through the universe. With them I seek the joys of heaven; with them I seek the fruits of earth. With them I engage in no business; with them I concoct no plots; with them I attempt nothing out-of-the-way. ... Every uncanny effect must be preceded by some uncanny cause. Alas! my sons and I have done nothing. It must be the will of God. Therefore I weep."

Shortly afterwards, when K'un was on his way to the Yen State, he was captured by brigands. To sell him as he was, would be no easy matter. To sell him without his feet would be easy enough. So they cut off his feet and sold him into the Ch'i State, where he became door-keeper to Duke Chü and had meat to his dinner for the rest of his life.

title.en: Hsü Yu Runs Away from Yao (Zhuangzi)

region.en: The hermit's path (symbolic pin: Jishan, Henan, China)
region.zh: 隱者之塗（象徵定位：河南箕山）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: Asked where he is going, Hsü Yu answers: away from Yao — who thinks of nothing but charity, and will become a laughing-stock of the world until future ages eat one another. Love and profit are born of charity and duty to one's neighbour; those who ignore them are few, those who make capital out of them are many.
summary.zh: 齧缺遇許由曰：子將奚之？曰：將逃堯——夫堯畜畜然仁，吾恐其為天下笑；後世其人與人相食與！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yeh Ch'üeh meeting Hsü Yu, said to him, "Where are you going?" "Away from Yao!" replied the latter. "What do you mean?" asked Yeh Ch'üeh. "Yao," said Hsü Yu, "thinks of nothing but charity. I fear he will become a laughing-stock to the world, and that in future ages men will eat one another.

"There is no difficulty in winning the people. Love them and they will draw near. Profit them and they will come up. Praise them and they will vie with one another. But introduce something they dislike, and they will be gone. ... Love and profit are born of charity and duty to one's neighbour. Those who ignore charity and duty to one's neighbour are few; those who make capital out of them are many. ... Yao knows that good men benefit the empire. But he does not know that they injure it. Only those on a higher level than good men know this."

title.en: The Two Kingdoms on the Snail's Horns (Zhuangzi)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: On a snail's left horn there is a kingdom called Aggression and on its right horn another called Violence, constantly fighting for territory — corpses by the thousands, pursuers away for fifteen days. Descend from boundless space to a kingdom with fixed boundaries, and in it is Wei, in Wei the city of Liang, and in Liang a prince — in what does he differ from Violence? Whew! cried the prince. Then Hui Tzŭ's tube-note: Yao and Shun, compared with Tai Chin Jen, are but whssh.
summary.zh: 有國於蝸之左角者曰觸氏，有國於蝸之右角者曰蠻氏；時相與爭地而戰，伏尸數萬——君之與蠻氏，亦猶是也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the snail-horn kingdoms are Zhuangzi's most-cited satire on war. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Prince Hui of Wei had made a treaty with prince Wei of Ch'i, which the latter broke. Thereupon prince Hui was wroth, and was about to send a man to assassinate him. When Hui Tzŭ heard of the ministers' war-plans, he introduced Tai Chin Jen to the prince. "There is a creature called a snail," said Tai Chin Jen. "Does your Highness know what I mean?" "I do," replied the prince. "There is a kingdom on its left horn," continued Tai Chin Jen, "ruled over by Aggression, and another on its right horn, ruled over by Violence. These two rulers are constantly fighting for territory. In such cases, corpses lie about by thousands, and one party will pursue the other for fifteen days before returning."

"Sire," replied Tai Chin Jen, "I beg you to regard it as fact. Does your Highness recognise any limit to space?" "None," said the prince, "It is boundless." "When, therefore, the mind descends from the contemplation of boundless space to the contemplation of a kingdom with fixed boundaries, that kingdom must seem to be of dimensions infinitesimally small?" "Of course," replied the prince. "Well then," said Tai Chin Jen, "in a kingdom with fixed boundaries there is the Wei State. In the Wei State there is the city of Liang. In the city of Liang there is a prince. In what does that prince differ from Violence?" "There is no difference," said the prince.

Thereupon Tai Chin Jen took his leave, and the prince remained in a state of mental perturbation, as though he had lost something. When Tai Chin Jen had gone, Hui Tzŭ presented himself, and the prince said, "Our friend is truly a great man. Sages are not his equal." "If you blow through a tube," replied Hui Tzŭ, "the result will be a note. If you blow through the hole in a sword-hilt, the result will be simply whssh. Yao and Shun have been belauded by mankind; yet compared with Tai Chin Jen they are but whssh."

title.en: The Sage Under a Menial's Garb on Mount I (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 孔子之楚，舍於蟻丘之漿（莊子）

region.en: The wine-shop of Mount I, Ch'u (Yicheng, Hubei, China)
region.zh: 蟻丘之漿（象徵定位：湖北宜城）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: Stopping at a wayside wine-shop on Mount I, Confucius sees a servant climb onto the roof: a Sage under the garb of a menial, who has drowned himself on dry land — I think 'tis I Liao of Shih-nan. Sent to call him, Tzŭ Lu finds the house empty; the hidden one has scorned the toady's words.
summary.zh: 孔子之楚，舍於蟻丘之漿。其鄰有夫妻臣妾登極者——是陸沉者也。是其言也，猥以人乎！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Confucius went to Ch'u, he stopped at a restaurant on Mount I. The servant to a man and his wife who lived next door, got up on top of the house. "Whatever is he doing up there?" asked Tzŭ Lu. "He is a Sage," replied Confucius, "under the garb of a menial. He buries himself among the people. He effaces himself at the wayside. Fame, he has none; but his perseverance is inexhaustible. Though his mouth speaks, his heart speaks not. He has turned his back upon mankind, not caring to abide amongst them. He has drowned himself on dry land. I think 'tis I Liao of Shih-nan."

Tzŭ Lu asked to be allowed to go and call him; but Confucius stopped him, saying, "No. He knows that I know what he is. He knows that I have come to Ch'u to recommend him to the prince. And he looks on me as a toady. Under the circumstances, as he would scorn to hear the words of a toady, how much more would he scorn to see him in the flesh! How could you keep him?" Tzŭ Lu went to see, but the house was empty.

title.en: Poh Chü Asks Lao Tzŭ to Wander the World (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 柏據學於老聃，請遊天下（莊子）

region.en: Lao Tzŭ's retreat (symbolic pin: Ku county, Bozhou, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 老聃之居（象徵定位：安徽亳州苦縣）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: The disciple Poh Chü begs Lao Tzŭ to wander the world with him. The world is just as you see it here, replies the Sage. Poh Chü explains that he would begin in Ch'i, viewing the dead bodies of malefactors, pushing them to make them rise, crying to God and bemoaning their lot — for honour and disgrace were set up, and evil followed; wealth was accumulated, and contentions began.
summary.zh: 柏據曰：請之齊，見其辜，推而強之，解其朝服而幕之——噫嘻！夫子亦知古之所謂亂者乎？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Poh Chü was studying under Lao Tzŭ. "Let us go," said he, "and wander over the world." "No," replied Lao Tzŭ, "the world is just as you see it here." But as he again urged it, Lao Tzŭ said, "Where would you go to begin with?" "I would begin," answered Poh Chü, "by going to the Ch'i State. There I would view the dead bodies of their malefactors. I would push them to make them rise. I would take off my robes and cover them. I would cry to God and bemoan their lot, as follows:--'O sirs, O sirs, there was trouble upon earth, and you were the first to fall into it!'

"I would say, 'Perhaps you were robbers, or perhaps murderers?'... Honour and disgrace were set up, and evil followed. Wealth was accumulated, and contentions began. Now the evil which has been set up and the contentions which have accumulated, endlessly weary man's body and give him no rest. What escape is there from this?"
